newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Nikkei slips, jarred by Wall Street tumble.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Nikkei slips, jarred by Wall Street tumble.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market's key index slipped below the key 19,000-point level in early morning trade on Monday, jarred by Friday's tumble on Wall Street.
After 38 minutes of trade, the Nikkei 225 average was down 467.64 points, or 2.42 percent, at 18,858.39. Its September futures were down 570 points at 18,870.

"Arbitrageurs sold cash stocks in response to Friday's weak closing of the Nikkei 225 futures in Chicago which was caused by the sharp fall in New York stocks," said an analyst at a major Japanese brokerage.
Arbitrageurs simultaneously trade stocks and their underlying futures, and profit from momentary discrepancies between the prices of the two instruments.
On Friday, the Dow tumbled 247.37 points to 7,694.66, its second-biggest point drop ever.
On Friday, before Wall Street opened, the Nikkei 225 average had gained 103.41 yen or 0.54 percent to end at 19,326.03, recovering from its own fall earlier last week.

Analysts had forecast Wall Street's tumble would spill over into Monday morning's trade in Tokyo because generally weak market sentiment would raise concern among global investors about the strength of Japanese equities.
Domestic issues are also weighing on the Tokyo market, with credit concerns pushing money into a limited number of blue-chip shares.
Worries about corporate credit risks have grown especially in the construction sector since the failure last month of contractor Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd.
There were no immediate signs that the market was reacting to another hefty jump in Japan's trade surplus.
The Ministry of Finance announced shortly before the market opened that Japan's overall customs-cleared trade surplus in July rose 69.7 percent from a year earlier.
The overall surplus came in at 849.08 billion yen, while the surplus with the United States grew 35.7 percent to 420.55 billion yen.
At Monday's exchange rate of around 118 yen to the dollar, the overall customs-cleared trade surplus was $7.19 billion, while the surplus with the United States was $3.56 billion.
July's sharp rise follows dramatic increases in April and May and is expected to add further kindling to trade tensions with Washington over the expanding surplus.

U.S. officials said they are concerned that Japan's surplus could keep rising into next year, particularly if car exports to the United States continue to increase while car imports continue to slow on weak demand in Japan.
Japanese officials say, however, that the pace of increase in the surplus will slow and that structural reforms in the economy will work to bring it down.
